parsed.n_justification: The Naches watershed spans ~800 km² with strong elevation gradients (352-1977m) creating distinct hydroclimatic zones. Twelve columns capture: (1) elevation gradient (low/mid/high: 400m, 900m, 1600m), (2) aspect variation (N/S facing slopes affecting snow dynamics), (3) soil texture diversity (coarse mountain soils vs. valley fine-loams), and (4) spatial recharge heterogeneity. This design balances computational feasibility with representation of dominant recharge controls (snowmelt timing, ET demand, infiltration capacity) across the watershed.

columns.notes: Riparian zone, shallow water table potential

elm_config.notes: 40-year spinup (1980-2019 repeated) to equilibrate deep soil moisture and water table, then 29-year analysis period (1990-2018). QCHARGE is the key recharge flux to unconfined aquifer. ZWT tracks water table depth for validation against USGS wells and Fan 2013. Bedrock enabled to represent shallow bedrock in mountains. Subgrid drainage and fmax parameterize saturation excess processes.

requires_capabilities: ELM with dynamic water table (ZWT) and unconfined aquifer recharge (QCHARGE)
Site-level meteorological forcing extraction for 12 Naches locations from DATM CLMNCEP
Soil texture and hydraulic parameter assignment from POLARIS or SSURGO for each column
Bedrock depth data from regional geology or topographic analysis
USGS well water table depth data for model validation
Fan et al. 2013 global water table depth product for prior comparison
Multi-decadal daily output storage and post-processing for steady-state analysis
Spatial interpolation or aggregation of 12-column results to watershed-scale recharge estimate
assumptions: Single-column simulations neglect lateral subsurface flow and watershed-scale groundwater convergence/divergence
Steady-state recharge defined as mean annual QCHARGE over 1990-2018 after 40-year spinup
Climate forcing (1980-2018) represents long-term average conditions despite potential non-stationarity
Soil hydraulic parameters from pedotransfer functions adequately represent subsurface properties
Bedrock depth and hydraulic conductivity estimates introduce uncertainty in deep drainage
No anthropogenic influences (pumping, irrigation return flow, land use change) explicitly represented
12 columns capture dominant spatial patterns but cannot resolve all local heterogeneity
Model structural uncertainty (e.g., Richards equation solver, runoff parameterizations) affects absolute recharge magnitudes
Validation against water table depth is indirect constraint on recharge (requires calibration of aquifer properties)
True steady-state may not exist given climate variability and transient trends in forcing data
